Lecture 13

A particle in space: orbital angular momentum

What this lecture does

Orbital angular momentum acts on wavefunctions in three dimensions. We decompose their space into finite-dimensional multiplets and prove that only integer spins occur. Harmonic polynomials give spherical harmonics, and central potentials reduce to a radial rule. The oscillator provides two counts of the same level.

  • Count the integer-spin multiplets in an oscillator level.

     Read the lecture →

  • Construct spherical harmonics from harmonic polynomials.

     Read the lecture →

  • Derive the radial rule away from the origin for smooth radial functions.

     Read the lecture →
Useful prerequisites
  • The finite well: a spectrum in two parts
  • States that stay and states that leave: decay

A molecule of HCl rotates almost as a rigid body: the distance ddd between the two nuclei hardly changes. The direction of its axis is a point of S2S^2S2, and its energy of rotation is L2/2IL^2/2IL2/2I, with the moment of inertia I=md2I=md^2I=md2 and the reduced mass mmm of the two nuclei. So the lines are equally spaced, at l+1l+1l+1 times the frequency ℏ/2πI\hbar/2\pi Iℏ/2πI. 13.6 The oscillator in space

Definition 13.9 (The oscillator in space). The Hamiltonian HHH of the isotropic oscillator of mass mmm and frequency ν\freqν, with s=ℏ/mνs=\sqrt{\hbar/m\freq}s=ℏ/mν​, is the operator made, as in Proposition 5.4, from the basis (hn1n2n3)(h_{n_1n_2n_3})(hn1​n2​n3​​) and the numbers ℏν(n1+n2+n3+32)\hbar\freq(n_1+n_2+n_3+\tfrac32)ℏν(n1​+n2​+n3​+23​).

By Proposition 5.4 it is self-adjoint. The rule −(ℏ2/2m)Δ+mν2∣x∣2/2-(\hbar^2/2m)\Delta+m\freq^2\abs x^2/2−(ℏ2/2m)Δ+mν2∣x∣2/2 is the sum of three rules (8.1), one in each variable, so it maps hn1n2n3h_{n_1n_2n_3}hn1​n2​n3​​ to ℏν(n1+n2+n3+32)hn1n2n3\hbar\freq(n_1+n_2+n_3+\tfrac32)h_{n_1n_2n_3}ℏν(n1​+n2​+n3​+23​)hn1​n2​n3​​, by Proposition 8.3. As in the proof of Theorem 8.8, HHH acts by this rule on S(R3)\mathcal S(\R^3)S(R3). The eigenspace of HHH for ℏν(N+32)\hbar\freq(N+\tfrac32)ℏν(N+23​) is ENE_NEN​, since a vector with this eigenvalue has no component on the other basis vectors.

Example 13.10 (The level NNN counted twice).

  1. By coordinates. The level ℏν(N+32)\hbar\freq(N+\tfrac32)ℏν(N+23​) has one basis vector for each triple (n1,n2,n3)(n_1,n_2,n_3)(n1​,n2​,n3​) with n1+n2+n3=Nn_1+n_2+n_3=Nn1​+n2​+n3​=N: for each n1n_1n1​ there are N−n1+1N-n_1+1N−n1​+1 choices of n2n_2n2​, so (N+1)(N+2)/2(N+1)(N+2)/2(N+1)(N+2)/2 in all.

  2. By rotations. By Theorem 13.5, ENE_NEN​ holds one multiplet of each spin l=N,N−2,…l=N,N-2,\dotsl=N,N−2,…, so its dimension is ∑(2l+1)\sum(2l+1)∑(2l+1) over these lll, an arithmetic progression with the step 444, whose sum is again (N+1)(N+2)/2(N+1)(N+2)/2(N+1)(N+2)/2. For example, the level N=2N=2N=2 has 6=5+16=5+16=5+1 states, of spins 222 and 000.

Each level ENE_NEN​ is a sum of whole multiplets (Theorem 13.5), as Quantum Mechanics I, Cor. 7.5, leads one to expect of a Hamiltonian that commutes with rotations. That the spins NNN and N−2N-2N−2 share a level is not forced by rotations. It comes from a larger symmetry of the oscillator, not used here, and Lecture 15 meets the same in hydrogen.

A particle in space

States: L2(R3)\Ltwo(\R^3)L2(R3) is an orthogonal sum of finite-dimensional multiplets of L\mathbf LL, made from polynomials times a Gaussian, and every spin is an integer (Theorem 13.5). Observables: the components of L=Q×P\mathbf L=Q\times PL=Q×P satisfy [L1,L2]=iℏL3\comm{L_1}{L_2}=\ii\hbar L_3[L1​,L2​]=iℏL3​ on S(R3)\mathcal S(\R^3)S(R3) (Proposition 13.4). Away from the origin, the rule of a central Hamiltonian on (u(r)/r)Ylμ(u(r)/r)Y_{l\mu}(u(r)/r)Ylμ​, with uuu smooth, is the radial rule HlH_lHl​ with the centrifugal term (Proposition 13.8). Measurement: a reading of L3L_3L3​ gives ℏμ\hbar\muℏμ with μ\muμ an integer, and a reading of L2L^2L2 gives ℏ2l(l+1)\hbar^2l(l+1)ℏ2l(l+1) with lll an integer; never ℏ/2\hbar/2ℏ/2.

Summary

  • Three dimensions: QjQ_jQj​, PjP_jPj​ and H0H_0H0​ are self-adjoint and act on S(R3)\mathcal S(\R^3)S(R3) by xjx_jxj​, −iℏ∂j-\ii\hbar\partial_j−iℏ∂j​ and −(ℏ2/2m)Δ-(\hbar^2/2m)\Delta−(ℏ2/2m)Δ (Proposition 13.2).
  • Orbital angular momentum: L=Q×P\mathbf L=Q\times PL=Q×P is symmetric on S(R3)\mathcal S(\R^3)S(R3) and satisfies [L1,L2]=iℏL3\comm{L_1}{L_2}=\ii\hbar L_3[L1​,L2​]=iℏL3​ (cyclic), and L3L_3L3​ generates the rotations about the x3x_3x3​-axis (Proposition 13.4).
  • The multiplets on functions: the oscillator’s level ENE_NEN​ is a sum of one multiplet of each spin N,N−2,…N,N-2,\dotsN,N−2,…, and these make up L2(R3)\Ltwo(\R^3)L2(R3); only integer spins occur (Theorem 13.5).
  • Spherical harmonics: the multiplet of spin lll in Pl\mathcal P_lPl​ is the harmonic polynomials, with top vector (x1+ix2)l(x_1+\ii x_2)^l(x1​+ix2​)l (Lemma 13.6); the YlμY_{l\mu}Ylμ​ form a basis of L2(S2)\Ltwo(S^2)L2(S2) (Theorem 13.7, cited).
  • Central potentials: away from the origin, the rule of H0+VH_0+VH0​+V on (u(r)/r)Ylμ(u(r)/r)Y_{l\mu}(u(r)/r)Ylμ​, with uuu smooth, is the radial rule with the term ℏ2l(l+1)/2mr2\hbar^2l(l+1)/2mr^2ℏ2l(l+1)/2mr2 (Proposition 13.8).

Lecture 15 solves the radial rule for hydrogen.
